title: Taylor Swift × X: Livestream Partnership
summary: Negotiation on a one-show livestream pilot on X. Taylor agreed to a single non-exclusive pilot contingent on three conditions: she owns the recording outright, X ships a named-harassment moderation control for the event, and Grok-verified ticketing runs a bot-resistance pilot for the tour presale. Revenue split set at 90/10 in Taylor's favor for the pilot.
decisions: Run a single livestream pilot: one show from the anthology tour, non-exclusive, no option clause
Taylor Swift retains full ownership of the recording and all derivative clips
Revenue split for the pilot is 90/10 in the artist's favor on pay-per-view and 70/30 on live ad inventory
X ships an event-scoped harassment filter and a named-account blocklist API before the show
Run a Grok-verified fan presale pilot for one tour date to test bot-resistant ticketing

action_items.task: Send the pilot term sheet reflecting the 90/10 split and full artist ownership of the recording
Deliver the moderation requirements document including the named-harassment filter spec
Have the X engineering team demo 4K livestream at 10 million concurrent viewers on a staging load test
Pick the pilot show date and the presale pilot city after reviewing the term sheet

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Taylor, Tree, thanks for coming in. I'll skip the pitch deck. X does about eight billion video views a day now, and live is the fastest-growing piece. I want the biggest live event in the platform's history, and honestly, nobody else on Earth can deliver that.

transcript.speaker: Taylor Swift
transcript.text: I appreciate the direct start, so I'll match it. I've watched artists get burned by platform deals for twenty years, and I've been the artist getting burned. So before we talk about the fun stuff, I have three non-negotiables, and if any of them is a problem we can save each other an hour.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Go.

transcript.speaker: Taylor Swift
transcript.text: One, I own the recording. Not a license, not a joint copyright — I own the masters of the stream, the VOD, and every clip, the same way I re-recorded four albums to own my catalog. Two, no exclusivity. This is one show, and I keep streaming rights everywhere else. Three, the harassment problem on your platform gets fixed for my fans before I bring seventy million of them to it in one night.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: One and two, yes, easily. The recording is yours, full stop — we make money on the event, not on owning your work. Non-exclusive is fine for a pilot; exclusivity only makes sense if the pilot works and we're both back at this table anyway. Three, tell me specifically what fixed means, because that word does a lot of work.

transcript.speaker: Tree Paine
transcript.text: I can be specific. When Taylor trends, there's a predictable wave — coordinated harassment of her, and worse, of individual fans. Teenagers with two hundred followers getting dogpiled. We track it. During the last tour announcement we logged spikes within ninety minutes of the post. Your current reporting tools resolve those cases in days. The event will last three hours.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Okay, that's a real product gap, not a policy debate, so let's treat it like engineering. What if we build an event-scoped mode — for the duration of the stream plus forty-eight hours, an ML filter tuned on the harassment patterns you've already logged, auto-limiting repeat offenders, plus an API so your team can push a blocklist of known bad actors directly instead of filing reports one at a time.

transcript.speaker: Taylor Swift
transcript.text: That's the right shape. But I need it to be real, not a press release. I want it live and tested before the show, and I want my team to have access during the event — a dashboard, not an email address.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Done. Tree, send us the requirements doc with the patterns you've logged and we'll build against it. If our safety team pushes back on the blocklist API I'll overrule them, it's a good feature anyway. If we don't ship it, you walk, that can literally be in the contract.

transcript.speaker: Tree Paine
transcript.text: It will be in the contract. You'll have the requirements document by the 10th.

transcript.speaker: Taylor Swift
transcript.text: Okay. Now the fun stuff. Tell me why X instead of the streamers. I've had offers from all of them, and they come with nine-figure guarantees and much less... unpredictability. You specifically are the unpredictability, I want to be clear.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Fair. Three reasons. First, scale of the live moment — a streamer gives you subscribers watching alone; X gives you the show and the global conversation about the show in one place. The second-screen behavior already happens on X during your tours, we're just merging the screens. Second, speed — we can ship custom features for your event in weeks. Third, money — no streamer will beat the split I'll give you, because I'm not trying to profit on the pilot, I'm trying to prove live at scale.

transcript.speaker: Taylor Swift
transcript.text: Then let's test that third claim. What's the split?

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Pay-per-view, 80/20 your favor. Ad inventory around the free tier, 50/50.

transcript.speaker: Taylor Swift
transcript.text: 90/10 and 70/30. You just said you're not trying to profit on the pilot — this is me taking you at your word, which I'm told is a thing you like. And my number accounts for the fact that I'm lending you the most reliable audience in entertainment to stress-test your infrastructure. If the servers fall over, it's my show that's ruined, not your quarter.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Ha. Okay, that's a fair point wrapped around a knife. 90/10 on PPV, 70/30 on ads, for the pilot only — if we go to a multi-show deal the economics get renegotiated from scratch. And in exchange, I want the load test to be real: we announce the stream on X first, one hour before anywhere else.

transcript.speaker: Taylor Swift
transcript.text: The announcement can go on X first. My fans find things in about four minutes anyway. Deal on the split.

transcript.speaker: Tree Paine
transcript.text: On infrastructure — what's the honest concurrent number you can hold? Her last tour livestream on cable-plus-streaming did about sixteen million across platforms. If she does a farewell-anthology show as a global free-plus-PPV event, internal projections say twenty-five million concurrent is possible. What's X actually held?

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Biggest live event so far peaked around nine million concurrent, and I'll be honest, we saw degraded video for about eight percent of viewers in the first ten minutes. Since then we've rebuilt the edge encoding and moved live delivery to our own CDN nodes in the top forty metros. The engineering team tells me thirty million concurrent at 1080p, ten million at 4K. I don't repeat engineering claims without a test, so: we'll run a staged load test at ten million synthetic viewers in 4K and your team can watch the dashboards live.

transcript.speaker: Taylor Swift
transcript.text: Good, because 'the site slowed down during my show' is a headline I've lived through with ticketing, and once was enough. Which brings me to the thing I actually came here wanting to talk about. Ticketing.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: I hoped you would. Go on.

transcript.speaker: Taylor Swift
transcript.text: The scalping problem is fundamentally a bot problem, and everyone in ticketing has failed at it for a decade. Verified fan systems leak. Half the resale markup ends up funding bot farms. You run a platform that fights bots at a scale nobody else does — I want to know if that tech transfers. If X can verify a human better than a ticketing company can, that's worth more to me than any livestream.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: It transfers. Grok runs behavioral bot detection across the whole platform — typing cadence, session patterns, device entropy, network fingerprints. It's a harder problem on X because bots there mimic years of account history; a presale is actually an easier, more bounded version. Here's my proposal: we run a Grok-verified presale pilot for one tour date. Fans verify through X, detection runs at queue entry, and we publish the results — what percentage of blocked entries were bots, what happened to resale prices for that date versus a control city.

transcript.speaker: Tree Paine
transcript.text: Publishing results cuts both ways. If it works, it embarrasses the incumbent ticketing partners we still have contracts with. We'd want control over the announcement framing.

transcript.speaker: Taylor Swift
transcript.text: I'm comfortable making enemies in ticketing, Tree, it's practically a hobby at this point. But yes — we control the framing, and we pick a mid-size market for the pilot, not a stadium city. If it fails, it fails quietly. If it works, we have leverage for the whole tour.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Agreed on both. One more thing from my side. Grok integration during the livestream — real-time multilingual captions, an AI concierge answering fan questions about the setlist. Tasteful, opt-in, no AI-generated content of you at all, that's a hard line for us too.

transcript.speaker: Taylor Swift
transcript.text: Captions yes, absolutely — that's genuinely great for international fans. The concierge, my team reviews everything it's allowed to say about me before it says it. And I want it in writing that no part of the stream trains any generative model. Not my face, not my voice, not the audio. My music has been scraped enough for one lifetime.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: In writing, agreed. The stream is contractually excluded from all training corpora. Honestly, the fact that you have to ask is an indictment of my industry. Okay — Tree, term sheet from our side by Friday the 7th. What else blocks a yes?

transcript.speaker: Tree Paine
transcript.text: Insurance and force majeure language, given the platform's, as Taylor said, unpredictability. If the platform has a global outage during the show, there's a make-good. And the pilot show date comes from our side once we see the term sheet — we're thinking one of the December indoor dates, smaller room, huge scarcity story.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: A small room broadcast to the whole planet — the contrast is the story. I love it. Make-good language is fine, our uptime this year has been solid but I'd take that bet anyway.

transcript.speaker: Taylor Swift
transcript.text: Then here's where I land. One show, non-exclusive, I own everything, 90/10, the safety tooling ships and is tested or I walk, the training-data exclusion is airtight, and we run the ticketing pilot in parallel because that's the part I suspect we'll both remember in five years. I'll pick the date and the presale city by the 14th.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Deal. I came in wanting a livestream and I'm leaving having possibly agreed to disrupt ticketing, which is a very on-brand outcome for this building. We'll get you the term sheet Friday and the load test by the 21st.

transcript.speaker: Taylor Swift
transcript.text: And Elon — announcement goes out on both our accounts simultaneously, coordinated to the minute. If I wake up to a surprise post at 3 a.m., the deal's off and I will write a song about it.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Understood. Coordinated to the minute. And for the record, the song would probably outperform the livestream, so I have every incentive to behave.
